title: Application permissions
text:
The permission-based access control model assigns access privileges for certain data objects to application. This is a derivative of the discretionary access control model. The access permissions are usually granted in the context of a specific user on a specific device. Permissions are often granted permanently with few automatic restrictions.

In some cases, permissions are implemented via an 'all-or-nothing' approach: a user is expected to either grant all the requested permissions in order to access the application, or else the user is completely barred from accessing that particular application. There remains a lack of transparency regarding exactly when each permission is used by a given program or application. Likewise, the same lack-of-transparency concern also applies to accessing the data protected by the permission access-control mechanism. Even if a user can revoke a permission, the app can blackmail a user by refusing to operate, for example by just crashing or asking user to grant the permission again in order to access the application.

The permission mechanism has been widely criticized by researchers for several reasons, including;

Intransparency of personal data extraction and surveillance, including the creation of a false sense of security;[1,2]

End-user fatigue of micro-managing access permissions, thereby leading to a fatalistic acceptance of surveillance and intransparency;[3]

Massive data extraction and personal surveillance carried out once the permissions have been granted (often by users who are unaware that behind-the-scenes surveillance is taking place).[4,5]

Some apps, such as XPrivacy and Mockdroid[6] spoof data in order to act as a measure for privacy. Further transparency methods include longitudinal behavioural profiling and multiple-source privacy analysis of app data access.[7,8]
